en: The Mahāgaṇapati Stotra composed by Śrī Rāghavacaitanya, together with a commentary (ṭippaṇī) written by his disciple: [Salutation] to Yoga, the abode of meditation for those who know yoga, whose pure intentions have had various distractions shaken off, and in whom the nectar-essence has manifested and spread through their meditation.
We worship that Supreme Plenum, matured as the very self of the elephant, which is rich with the spreading fragrance of the sweetness of consciousness floating upon bliss.
We worship that Supreme Brahman, the Infinite, who has transformed Himself into that form—the elephant-faced one—whose face is like that of an elephant possessing tusks (dantāvala).
Of what nature is He?
He is floating upon the bliss of Brahman (ānanda).
By implication, the meaning is that he is non-different from Pūrṇānanda.
Such is the awakening (bodha) by which his own nature is said to consist of consciousness and bliss (cidānandamaya).

The phenomenal world (prapañca), which is of the nature of its illusory manifestation (vivarta), is metaphorically described as a burst of sweet fragrance; therefore, [the nature] is "rich" (medura) with that.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is the yoga of those who know yoga.
Of what nature are those who know yoga?

And for those who dwell in such abodes as mountain caves— abodes characterized by a pervasive and spreading meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), wherein the nectar-essence of peace has emerged within a pure disposition, precisely because their various attachments have been shaken off.

May there be prostration to that Lord of the Gaṇas whom they know as following the forms of Tārā, Śrī, Paraśakti, Kāmā, and Vasudhārā; he who is entreated by the passionate, first being addressed as "O Bestower," then as "O Giver of Boons," and [prayed to] with the words "Bring all people under my control, O Master! and is constantly worshipped with Svāhā and other offerings.
He extracts the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati: *tāra* is the *praṇava* (om), *śrī* is the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī,
and *paraśakti* is the seed-syllable of Māyā.

The construction is as follows: "May there be salutation to that Lord of the Gaṇas, whom practitioners know as the syllable 'Yaṃ', which follows upon the five forms of seeds— namely, Desire (kāma) being the seed of desire, and the Earth (vasudhā) being the seed of the ground."

He who is constantly worshipped with the powers of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and so forth, is first addressed by the afflicted, passionate person as "O Bestower" (*vara*), and then entreated as "O Giver of Boons" (*varada*). He states the very petition: "O Lord, bring all people under my control."
By the phrase "with *svāhā* and so forth," it is indicated that the mantra ends with *svāhā*.
Here, the word *adhipadam* (the word for the lord) and the word *sarvam* (all) are stated [separately] in accordance with the requirements of the meter;
however, in the actual mantra, *gaṇapataye* and likewise *sarvajanam* constitute a single compound word.
And the word "svāmin" is external to the mantra.

I worship Him upon that imperishable lotus—the root of the wish-fulfilling tree—situated on a pedestal made of great jewels at the base of the wish-fulfilling tree; which tree abounds in the singular richness of the fragrance of groves of celestial trees on an island in the ocean whose waters are agitated by waves kissing the expanse of the clouds; and which lotus is graced with a pericarp formed by the arrangement of a triangle within a hexagon.

By the edges—that is, the extremities—of the billowing great waves, the mass of clouds was embraced; thus, in this ocean of sugarcane juice, there is a grove of celestial trees such as the *pārijāta* and others.

By their fragrance, a jewel-encrusted island—a piece of land situated in the midst of the waters—is nourished. At the foot of a *kalpavṛkṣa* tree located upon that island is a pedestal made of great gems.
Therein, within a lotus of imperishable syllables (*akṣarāmbhoruha*)—a *mātṛkā-kamala* well-known in the Tantras—which possesses a six-cornered triangle at its center, [is the Goddess].
I worship this great Gaṇapati.

We seek refuge in the Great Gaṇapati, the Lord of the Universe, who resembles a ruby; whose hands hold a discus, a spear, a sword, a bow, a mace, a citron, a conch, a grain of rice, a lotus, a noose, and a lotus; whose trunk-tip grasps a jar; and who is embraced by his beloved, whose hand holds a lotus and who is adorned with shimmering jewel ornaments.
The discus is well known;
the spear is the trident;
the bow is the sugarcane bow, the *rasālaka*.
The mace is well-known;
the citron is the *mātuliṅga*;
and the "twice-born" is one's own tooth.
The "tip of rice" (vrīhyagra) is the cluster of a *śāli* grain;
the *utpala* is well known; and the noose (*pāśa*) and lotus (*paṅkaja*) are also well known.

We pray for the Great Gaṇapati, the Lord of All, whose ten weapons are thus held in his hands; upon the tip of whose trunk stands an alert jar—a golden vessel filled with jewels; and who, possessing a ruby-like complexion and a crimson luster, is embraced by his beloved with her lotus-hand on his right side.

May that Lord of the Gaṇas perpetually bestow prosperity— he who, under the guise of his pair of cheeks reddened with vermilion and bearing hanging bees thick with the water of his charity, bears two plaques of praise as beautiful as rubies, inscribed with the letters of the performance of the rites desired by the three worlds.

May that Lord Gaṇapati, who bears two frontal globes (kumbha) that are exceedingly full with the water of his generosity and the ichor of his rut, which are pervaded by hovering bees (rolamba) swarming about; which are reddened by vermilion (sindūra); and which, under the guise of those globes, possess the beauty of the letters that grant the three worlds their desires—letters charming as they ordain the welfare of the three worlds, resembling rubies (padmarāga)—may he, the God of the hosts, perpetually bestow prosperity.
Just as one writes letters with red powder on a wooden board smeared with clay and water,
so too it is said that there are bees upon the surface of the jar, which is smeared with the water of charity and colored with vermilion.

May the luster of the tusks of Ganesha—whose beauty eclipses the pride of the shimmering clusters of chowries that possess the hue of the waves of the Ocean of Milk as it is helplessly churned by the whirling Mount Mandara; who serve as a thick shower of sandalwood paste for the beauties of the quarters; and who smear the sky with their unrestrained expansion—take refuge in my mind.
May the splendors of Heramba’s tusks take refuge in the mind.
Of what nature are they?
They are like the masses—the foremost parts—of the waves and billows of the Ocean of Milk, which depend upon Mount Mandara as it revolves from its whirling motion.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
They utterly humble the pride of the beauty of the intermingling of waving chowries.
"Intermingling" (vyatikara) means entanglement (vyatiṣaṅga).
The phrase beginning with "dikkāntā" (the beloved of the quarters) is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
"Ghanasāra" means camphor.
Likewise, "svacchandaprasarapraliptaviyatas" refers to spaces in the sky filled with extensive movement, where the atmosphere is smeared by the free expansion [of the camphor].
By this, the multiplicity of splendors is manifested.

Victorious for a long time are the splendors of Heramba’s body, intermingled with clusters of pearls and lovely with the radiance of blooming heaps of rubies; resembling young sprouts embraced by thick coils of conch shells, they are like companions of the twilight slowly drifting on the waves of a flood of moonlight, scattered with the rays from his tusks.
Resplendent with the radiance of clusters of glowing rubies interspersed with clusters of pearls, lovely and enchanting,
resembling vast stretches of coral joined with shells;
they are the companions of the twilight, who slowly drift upon the waves of the flood of moonlight, being equal to her in beauty.
May such bodily splendors of Heramba, pervaded by the rays from his tusks, be victorious for all time!

Victorious is the Lord, the leader of the Gaṇas, who honors the practitioners by pouring forth from a golden jar held at the tip of his trunk—a jar from which a multitude of various jewels flows; he sports with the swaying of his ears as they are set in motion to drive away the bees greedy for the fragrance and delight of his gifts.

With a multitude of pearls, rubies, and other jewels held within golden jars carried on his trunk—which, due to their great volume, overflowed and spilled even outside—he honored millions of practitioners and increased the prosperity of countless devotees.
[The passage begins with] "Dāna... and so forth.

Āmoda means fragrance and joy; for the purpose of driving away and exorcising [evil], he performs the sport of swaying his ears as they manifest [their power]. Victorious is the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God!
I bow to Heramba, before whom Madhuripu bears his conch and discus together with Śrī holding a lotus at the base of the Śāṇḍilya tree;
and at the foot of the Nyagrodha tree, Śambhu stands with the daughter of the mountain on his left, while she on his right bears an auspicious axe and trident, and he holds a noose and a goad.

At the foot of the *śāṇḍilya* tree, beneath a *bilva* tree, stands Madhuripu Viṣṇu, who carries the well-known conch and discus along with Śrī, who holds a lotus in her hand, positioned in front of that Great Gaṇapati;
likewise, to his south, at the base of a banyan tree (*nyagrodha*), resides Śambhu Śiva, who, together with Adrisutā Pārvatī— who is accompanied by the noose and goad— carries an axe and a trident.
Behind him, resting beneath a *pippala* tree, was the Lord of Rati (Kāmadeva), who, together with his consort Rati holding a blue lotus, carried a bow made of sugarcane and five flower-arrows;
and to the left, beneath a *priyaṅgu* tree, was the blessed Lord Varāha with the goddess Dharaṇī, who held a cluster of rice stalks and a parrot in her raised hand.

To the west of the deity, beneath a *pippala* tree, is Kāmadeva, the Lord of Rati; he holds a bow made of sugarcane and five arrows made of flowers, together with Rati, who carries an *utpala* lotus. To his left, beneath a *priyaṅgu* tree, is the famous Blessed One, the Boar (*Kroḍa-varāha*), together with Dharaṇī, who holds in one hand a cluster of rice stalks from which a parrot is rising, and in the other, the awn of *kalama* rice.
"I bow to Heramba"—thus it is connected with what precedes.

In the six corners of the hexagon are the six elephant-faced ones, bearing nooses, goads, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; they are accompanied by female attendants and possess the luster of vast masses of great red jewels.
Āmoda is in front, Pramoda and Sumukha are on his two sides, Durmukha is behind him, and Vighna—who is called Vighnakarta—is at his rear flank.
On the six corners and the six ridges of the hexagonal pedestal, six elephant-faced deities are to be meditated upon.
Of what nature are they?
They hold in their hands nooses, goads, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

"Companions of young women" (*pramadāsakhāḥ*) means those who have wives as their companions; that is the meaning. They possess a luster and splendor like a broad and great heap of *mahāśoṇa* gems—that is, rubies (*padmarāga*).
If the reading is *'pṛthumahāḥ'* ending in a visarga, then it is a separate word:
"those whose greatness (*mahaḥ*) is vast (*pṛthuḥ*)."
There is also a word *maha* ending in the vowel *a*.
He states their names: in front, at the eastern corner, is Āmoda;
and on both sides of that Āmoda are Pramoda and Sumukha.
In relation to the previously conceived eastern direction, *pramoda* is in the southeast corner;
likewise, *sumukha* is in the northeast corner—this is the meaning.
Behind, in the west corner, is *durmukha*.
The one named Vighna, meaning "Obstacle," is on one side; the one named Vighnakarta, meaning "Obstacle-maker," is on the second side.
That is to say, one is in the southwest corner (nairṛtyakoṇa), and the other is in the northwest (vāyavya).

Āmodā and the other beloveds of Gaṇeśvara reside there eternally, their languid glances steeped in the flavor of embracing their lovers; from them come Siddhi, Samṛddhi, Kānti—who is likewise celebrated in the Kalpas as Madanāvatī—and also Madadravā and Drāviṇī, who are worshipped.
Those whose eyes are languid and impassioned because they know the taste of embracing their own beloved husbands;
who stand near those six—the spouses of fragrance and the others mentioned in the previous verse—they should be meditated upon.
Their names are as follows: Siddhi, ...
Samṛddhi, Kānti, and Madanāvatī.
Madadravā and Drāviṇī.
Then the Earth embraced him, and Vasumatī [embraced] Sitā and Lohita; on his two sides shone the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, raining down wealth.

Following his limbs were the Mothers, and all around them were Indra and the others who dwell in the lotus; outside of them were the thunderbolt and other weapons, possessing the brilliance of the falling fire of time.

One should perform the meditation on those two well-known treasures named Śaṅkha and Padma, which are white and red in color respectively, showering wealth, embraced by Vasudhā and Vasumatī in succession, and shining on the sides of the hexagon; this is the meaning. Following the meditation on the treasures, one should meditate upon the heart and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
All around, the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī should be meditated upon.

Outside the hexagon, on an eight-petaled lotus, the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) such as Indra and others are to be visualized; and outside of them, in their very vicinity, the weapons of Indra and the rest—such as the thunderbolt (vajra)—which possess the nature of blazing forms and the radiance of a falling fire, should be meditated upon.

Homage to that Supreme One, whose body is the reality of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest; who possesses radiant splendor, having scattered the entire host of demon armies with the sound "huṃ"; who has destroyed the waves of all worldly existence through the surge of awakening into the single essence of bliss; and whose charming majesty shines everywhere.
"I bow to Heramba" (9/10).
By these two verses, [it is said]: "to him whose body or form consists of the essential natures of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others";
by the word "others" (ādipada), Kāma and Varāha are included.
To the one whose radiant splendor has dispelled the entire host of asura armies by a mere *huṃ* sound;
to the one who is "Bliss" (*Ānanda*), who has cast away all full waves of existence with the surging ripples of the manifestation of unsurpassed happiness.
The waves are the six transformations of existence (bhāvavikāra),
and they are: it is born, it exists,
It increases, it transforms, and it diminishes.
Regarding the phrase "it perishes":

some say it refers to that from which the waves—the mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) produced by the six sense organs—of all practitioners are destroyed by the surging waves of the realization of the single flavor of bliss (*ānandaikarasa*).
Others hold that by the word "waves" (*ūrmi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, as well-known in the Yoga scriptures, are meant.
Salutation to that Supreme One, who is other than this world, whose splendor is everywhere expanding, charming, and beautiful.

O King, may that elephant-faced one—who possesses a pre-eminent row of jewels equal to the sun as it moves across the millions upon millions of crowns of the vast multitude of gods, asuras, and men who are devoted to his service; and whose toe-nails shine with a splendor like a royal lustration—grant me, who possess pure vision, a beautiful and stable state of supreme well-being.
Those who possess eagerness (*hevāka*)— that is, longing— for service;
it refers to the desire "May I be first, may I be first," which is to say, a competitive scramble for precedence (*ahaṃpūrvikā*).

O you of stainless vision, O wise ones! That well-known elephant-faced one, whose face is like the ocean, shines with the radiance of his toenails— which are the companions of the glorious lustration (*nīrājana*) and the beauty of the waving of lights (*ārātrika*)— a splendor consisting of streams of light from rows of jewels equal to the sun, moving in close formation at the tip of the multitude of gods, asuras, and men, a multitude whose crowns are brilliantly blazing, reaching the very limit (*koṭi*) of their number.
May my beautiful, delightful, stable, most steadfast, and auspicious [Lord] grant me well-being;
or rather, "mine" is a qualification for "the one of pure vision," namely,
"by the one of pure vision."
But in this reading, the meaning is that he should bestow welfare by means of a gentle glance.

Whoever praises Mahāgaṇeśa profusely with this hymn— which contains the garland of mantras, both manifest and secret, and which possesses most vivid consciousness— for him this triple world becomes submissive.
By the phrase "a most vivid consciousness," the quality of grace (*prasāda*) is indicated in this hymn; it is "abundant" and occurs "repeatedly.
The rest is clear.
Thus ends the *Mahāgaṇapatistotra*, composed by the illustrious and eminent wandering ascetic teacher Śrī Rāghavacaitanya, together with the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*) written by his disciple.
